# Results — Study 49 (Black-Gold): does oil predict the stock market? 2000–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly returns of **WTI crude (CL=F)**, the
**S&P 500 (^GSPC)** and the **13-week T-bill** (^IRX, the cash leg), built from daily closes resampled
to month-end on a verified hole-free grid: 2000-09 → 2026-05, **309 months, zero interior holes** — every
calendar month of tradable oil-futures data. Driesprong et al. (2008): last month's oil return forecasts
this month's equity return, negatively. As-of 2026-06-01; inputs fingerprint `5b97b7d871ee`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `NONE` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Replicates out of sample"? `BUSTED`

The famous oil-predicts-stocks result **does not survive into the era you'd trade it**. Regressing this
month's equity return on last *calendar* month's oil return gives a slope of **−0.001 (t = −0.03)** —
as close to exactly zero as a regression gets. A timing rule that holds equities after oil falls (and
earns the T-bill in cash) makes **Sharpe 0.32** against buy-and-hold's **0.37** (excess of T-bill, both
legs) while giving up a quarter of the compound return. And no sub-period saves it: 2000–2008 has the
Driesprong sign but no significance (t = −0.9), 2009-on is positive and just as dead. `BUSTED`.

## Data stamp

- **Pair**: WTI (CL=F) + S&P 500 (^GSPC) + T-bill (^IRX) monthly, 2000-09 → 2026-05, **309 months,
  0 interior holes**, as-of 2026-06-01, fingerprint `5b97b7d871ee`
- **Construction**: daily closes resampled to month-end (last close of each calendar month). Yahoo's
  native monthly CL=F feed is full of holes (89 of 310 months missing on a 2026 pull) and silently
  mis-lagged the signal by 2–3 months in dozens of cases; the daily route has none, and
  `fetch_pair` asserts the grid hole-free on every read. *(An earlier run of this study used the gapped
  feed — its headline slope of +0.017 "wrong sign" was an artifact of that mis-alignment.)*

## No predictive relationship — the slope is zero

| regress equity_t on oil_(t−1), calendar lag | value |
|---|---|
| slope | **−0.001** (Driesprong: negative *and significant*) |
| correlation | −0.002 |
| t-stat | **−0.03** |
| n | 308 |

A t of −0.03 is the cleanest nothing on the bench: last month's oil return carries no information at all
about this month's S&P return. Whatever Driesprong found in 1973–2003, the relationship is absent on
every calendar month of tradable oil-futures data.

## …and the timing rule trails buy-and-hold, like-for-like

Cash months earn the rolled 13-week T-bill; Sharpe is **excess of T-bill on both legs**.

| | CAGR | Sharpe (excess) | max-DD | time in market |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| oil timing (long after oil falls, T-bill in cash) | +4.8% | **0.32** | −44% | 44% |
| buy & hold S&P | +6.5% | **0.37** | −53% | 100% |

Even with the cash leg properly credited, conditioning equity exposure on last month's oil gives up
1.6%/yr of compounding and a slice of risk-adjusted return — you sit out 56% of the time to dodge a
danger the regression says isn't there. (Raw Sharpes tell the same story: 0.47 vs 0.49.)

## It was never significant in the modern sample

| | slope | t | n |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2000–2008 | −0.042 | −0.9 | 99 |
| 2009–on | +0.006 | +0.2 | 208 |

The early sub-period leans the right (negative) way but is nowhere near significant; the last 17 years
flip the sign and stay dead. No sub-period shows the negative, significant relationship the strategy
needs.

## The honest takeaway

"Oil predicts the stock market" is a `MIRAGE` on every calendar month of tradable data: the predictive
slope is exactly zero (t = −0.03), and the timing rule trails buy-and-hold even after its cash leg is
paid the T-bill. The original 1973–2003 result doesn't replicate out of sample — a textbook reminder
that a documented predictability is a hypothesis about the *future*, and this one failed it. `NONE`,
`MIRAGE`, `BUSTED`.
